questions.title: Why did the court hold that only the Minnesota Commissioner, and not the employee, can recover § 181.101 wage-payment penalties?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the interaction between Minn. Stat. § 181.171 and § 181.101. Section 181.171 seems to let an employee bring a civil action for violations of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act and says the employer is liable for “compensatory damages and other appropriate relief,” plus any “civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated.” But the Eighth Circuit still says Cohen personally could not seek the “average daily wage penalties” under § 181.101 because that section talks about the Commissioner serving a demand and collecting the penalty. Why doesn't § 181.171 itself make those penalties privately recoverable once the employee proves a § 181.101 violation?

questions.title: How can an employee still have a live claim for civil penalties after being paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages?
questions.question_body: On the MFLSA claim, Cohen stipulated that he had already been paid all overtime wages and all liquidated damages he claimed he was owed. The remaining dispute was over statutory penalties, which everyone agrees would be paid to the Commissioner rather than to Cohen himself. I thought a plaintiff usually needs some personal stake in the relief sought. The panel cites Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw and says civil penalties can still redress a plaintiff by deterring ongoing violations, but I'm not seeing how that works when the money does not go to the plaintiff. What is the theory of redressability here?

questions.title: What is the difference between standing and mootness in the court's discussion of the MFLSA penalties issue?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the court has a “serious concern regarding our jurisdiction” over Cohen's request for MFLSA penalties. It then discusses both standing and mootness, saying standing must exist at the start of the case and mootness concerns whether that personal interest continues throughout the litigation. I'm struggling to separate those concepts in this case. Is the idea that Cohen may have had standing when Consilio was still using the allegedly unlawful overtime policy, but the case could become moot if the policy was later abandoned? Or is there also a threshold question whether he ever had standing at all to pursue penalties payable only to the government?

questions.title: Why did the Eighth Circuit vacate and remand the MFLSA ruling instead of just deciding the penalties issue on the merits?
questions.question_body: The district court granted summary judgment to Consilio on the MFLSA claim, and the court of appeals did not say Cohen actually wins on penalties. Instead, it vacated and remanded for the district court to determine its own jurisdiction. Why couldn't the Eighth Circuit resolve that itself? Was it because there was an unresolved factual dispute about whether Consilio's overtime policy was still in place, which matters for mootness under the voluntary-cessation doctrine? Or was the problem that the parties had not adequately briefed standing/jurisdiction?

questions.title: What effect did the parties' stipulation have on the case after Consilio paid the overtime and liquidated damages?
questions.question_body: The parties stipulated that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages he alleged were due, and they also agreed that the “most expedient and efficient path forward” was for the district court to decide summary judgment before further discovery or litigation. Since Cohen originally sued on behalf of himself and a putative class, I'm confused about what this stipulation did procedurally. Did it effectively narrow the case to a pure legal dispute about penalties and other remedies for Cohen individually? And does a stipulation like this risk waiving factual development that might have mattered later, especially on things like whether the challenged overtime policy was still ongoing?

questions.title: Why was the Minnesota Wage Theft Act claim treated as waived or unsupported on appeal?
questions.question_body: For the MWTA claim, Cohen argued that Consilio failed to provide the required notice of a change in its overtime policy under Minn. Stat. § 181.032. The Eighth Circuit says Cohen received all pay owed and “points to no statutory authority allowing for civil penalties under this statute,” and then says that with “no meaningful argument in support of reversal,” it will not disturb the dismissal. Is this saying the claim failed on the merits because the statute does not create a private penalty remedy, or is it saying the issue was waived on appeal because Cohen's brief did not develop the argument enough? I'm trying to understand whether this is a substantive holding or mainly an appellate briefing/default rule.

questions.title: When does changing the requested injunction in summary judgment briefing become an improper new claim under Rule 15?
questions.question_body: Cohen apparently asked for certain specific forms of injunctive relief in his complaint, but later argued in summary judgment that he should get an order requiring Consilio to rescind the 2019 overtime policy. The court says that issue was not properly before it because new claims must be raised through an amended complaint, not opposition briefs. I'm not sure where the line is here. If a plaintiff already pleaded a claim for injunctive relief, why isn't a different formulation of the injunction just a new remedy theory rather than a new claim? What made this change significant enough that Rule 15 was required?
